summaries.example: Imagine seeing a busy playground all at once. At first, you may notice many colors and sounds but not understand each one. If you want to find your friend, your need gives you a reason to pay attention to a red coat. Condillac thought experience teaches us where to look, what to remember, and how to think about what we sense.
summaries.summary: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac was an eighteenth-century philosopher who asked how the mind grows from experience. He argued that sensations—such as colors, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches—are the beginning of mental life. We are not simply born knowing how to focus, remember, imagine, or reason. Experience, helped by pleasure, pain, and our needs, teaches us these activities. Condillac explored this idea with a thought experiment about a human-shaped statue that gains its senses one at a time. A smell, for example, might first be felt simply as part of the statue’s own experience. Touch could then teach it about its body, solid things, and space outside itself. Later, language would help it name ideas, guide attention, remember absent things, and think more carefully. Condillac also wrote about animals, morality, government, trade, and the problems in his own theory. His account changed between his earlier Essay and later Treatise, especially on whether vision gives us depth immediately and whether unnoticed parts of sensations can guide perception.
key_ideas: Condillac argued that experience does more than give us information. It teaches us how to pay attention, remember, imagine, judge, and reason.
He used a pretend human-shaped statue that slowly receives senses to ask how a mind could learn about itself and the outside world.
Touch helps the statue learn that there are solid objects and space outside its own body.
Language helps people remember more, think about complicated ideas, and learn from one another.
Condillac believed animals can feel and learn habits, but humans develop further through richer language and cooperation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Condillac’s work asks a question that still matters: how do babies and learners develop abilities that seem ordinary to adults? His answer connects sensing, learning, language, teaching, and society. It also reminds us that a theory can be creative while still having difficulties. For example, critics questioned how sensation alone could explain memory, free choice, or the difference between an immaterial mind and extended sensations.

important_terms.definition: The view that our experiences through the senses help build our ideas and mental abilities.
Condillac’s view that sensation is the starting point for all our thinking and learning.
Focusing the mind on one part of what we are experiencing.
A sign or word we learn to use for an idea or thing.
The idea that a person or animal can feel and think, even though it may not be made of physical matter.

questions_to_think_about: Do you notice everything around you, or do your goals help you choose what to notice?
Could someone learn what a cube is using sight alone, or would touch help?
How do words help you remember something that is not in front of you?
Are habits always inborn, or can they be learned?
What might be difficult about explaining every thought as a result of sensation?

summaries.example: Suppose a student enters a laboratory filled with instruments, colored liquids, sounds, and written labels. The student’s attention is not spread evenly: an urgent assignment and previous experience make some features stand out. Later, a diagram or word can bring an apparatus to mind even when it is absent. For Condillac, this illustrates how needs direct attention, repeated experience supports imagination, and instituted signs extend memory and reflection. But it also raises a problem: the present experience of a remembered image does not by itself explain how the mind represents something as past.
summaries.summary: Étienne Bonnot de Condillac developed a radical empiricism usually called sensationism. Against views that allowed innate ideas or principles, he also questioned innate mental abilities. Sensation, on his account, is not merely passive input: experience teaches the mind how to attend, remember, imagine, abstract, judge, reason, and form desires. This gives his philosophy a developmental and pedagogical character. His famous statue thought experiment asks what a being with senses acquired in isolation could learn. Smell may initially be experienced without any distinction between the sensation and the self. The sequence of sensations can generate an awareness of temporal endurance, while touch—especially the contrast between touching one’s own body and another object—can lead to judgments about bodily extension and external things. Other senses are then referred to objects through learned regularities. In the Essay, Condillac resisted the claim that depth must be learned through touch; in the Treatise, he revised this position and accepted that perception can involve inferences and unnoticed aspects of sensation. Language is equally important. Natural cries and gestures are not innately understood, but their recurring associations can support deliberately instituted signs. These signs permit memory, naming of complex ideas, regulation of attention, and reflection. Language thus serves as an analytic method: by decomposing signs, speakers and interpreters decompose ideas, and each process improves the other. Condillac also argues that animals possess sensation and pre-linguistic reflection, while human language, imitation, and social cooperation permit greater intellectual development. His later discussions connect needs and value with commerce and defend freer exchange,,
key_ideas: Condillac rejects both innate ideas and, more radically, innate cognitive abilities. Experience is supposed to teach attention, imagination, judgment, reasoning, desire, and their proper use.
His “statue” thought experiment traces a possible development from isolated sensation to self-awareness, bodily and external spatial awareness, and perception of objects.
The Treatise revises the Essay: Condillac later allows unconscious inference and maintains that a sensation may contain features of which the subject is not yet aware.
Touch is central because comparisons between touching oneself and touching another object are meant to lead to judgments about bodily extension and external objects.
Language develops from natural cries and gestures toward instituted signs and articulated speech. It both expresses analysis and makes more refined analysis possible.
Condillac extends his theory to morality and political economy, while critics identify tensions concerning external-world knowledge, materialism, memory, and liberty.
summaries.why_it_matters: Condillac offers an early account of cognitive development that links perception, learning, language, education, and social life. He also shows why explaining the mind from experience alone is difficult. The SEP discussion identifies serious tensions: his theory of perception seems to presuppose extended sense organs while remaining uncertain about material objects; his extended sensations sit uneasily with an immaterial mind; and his accounts of memory and liberty may rely on capacities not fully derived from sensation. These problems help clarify the difference between a strong claim that sensation produces every mental power and a weaker claim that experience teaches us how to use powers.

important_terms.definition: The doctrine that knowledge and mental development arise from experience rather than innate ideas or abilities; Condillac gives sensation a particularly fundamental role.
Condillac’s radical form of empiricism, according to which sensation supplies not only knowledge but instruction in using cognitive and conative capacities.
A mental operation that selects some contents of experience for clearer awareness, initially guided by pleasure, pain, needs, and interests.
A sensation or circumstance that becomes associated with another and prompts its imagination; Condillac distinguishes accidental, natural, and instituted signs.
A deliberately established sign used to stand for an experience or idea, making more controlled memory, reflection, and communication possible.
A method of explaining complex ideas by breaking them into simpler, ordered elements; Condillac treats well-formed language, especially algebra, as an analytic instrument.
The view that the mind is not spatially extended, even though Condillac also describes sensations such as color as extended.

questions_to_think_about: Can a present sensory state alone explain awareness that something happened in the past?
If color is both a sensation and extended, how can it modify an unextended mind?
Does learning to use a voluntary sign really give a person control over thought, or is another account needed?
How does Condillac’s later treatment of unconscious inference alter the stronger version of his empiricism?
Can language be both a product of analysis and a condition that makes further analysis possible?

summaries.example: Imagine learning a new sport. At first, many movements and sounds happen at once. You begin to notice the coach’s most important signal because you want to improve. Repeated practice connects that signal with an action. Later, a short word such as “pass” can remind you what to do even when the coach is silent. Condillac would say that needs, experience, attention, habits, and language work together—but he would still need to explain how a present memory can be about the past.
summaries.summary: Condillac was an Enlightenment philosopher who developed a theory called sensationism. He began with the idea that the mind receives sensations through the senses, but he went beyond many other empiricists: he argued that experience also teaches us how to perform mental activities. We learn to direct attention, remember, imagine, compare, judge, reason, and form goals. Pleasure and pain help guide this learning because we focus on what seems useful or harmful. To explore how this development might happen, Condillac imagined a human-shaped statue that gains senses one at a time. A being with only smell might first experience itself simply as a smell, without an idea of an outside object or even a separate self. Repeated sensations could lead to an awareness of continuing through time. Touch could then help it distinguish its own body from other solid things and develop an idea of space. Condillac’s views about vision changed. In his earlier Essay, he argued that newly sighted people would perceive extended shapes immediately. In his later Treatise, he held that depth is learned through touch and associations, even though a sensation may contain information that the person does not yet notice. Language gives human thought another major advantage. Natural cries and gestures are produced by our constitution, but their meanings must be learned. People can turn such signs into shared, instituted signs and later into spoken and written language. These signs make it easier to remember absent things, control attention, and analyze complicated ideas. Condillac also discussed animals, morality, commerce, and government. key_ideas: Condillac argued that experience teaches people not only what things are like but also how to use mental abilities such as attention, imagination, judgment, and reasoning.
His imagined statue begins with sensations and gradually develops a sense of self, a body, space, and external objects.
He changed his view between two major works: he first defended immediate visual depth, then accepted that depth perception develops through experience and unconscious inference.
Pleasure, pain, needs, and interests guide attention. What we repeatedly notice can support habits, memory, and imagination.
Language grows from cries and gestures into shared signs. Words allow people to remember absent things, name complex groups, and reflect on ideas.
Condillac thought animals can sense, compare, and form habits, while humans gain greater abilities through language, imitation, and cooperation.
summaries.why_it_matters: Condillac’s philosophy helps explain why learning is more than collecting information. It involves training attention, forming habits, using signs, and learning from other people. His theory also shows how philosophers test a big idea by examining its difficult cases. If sensation is the source of all thought, how do we get memory of the past, voluntary choice, or reliable knowledge of an outside world? Condillac’s answers changed over time and remained open to criticism.

important_terms.definition: The belief that experience, especially sense experience, is the main source of knowledge.
Condillac’s stronger version of empiricism, which treats sensation as the basis from which mental abilities develop.
Choosing one part of experience to notice more clearly than the rest.
A learned connection in which one thing brings another idea or experience to mind.
A deliberately created word, gesture, or mark used to stand for an idea or experience.
A way of breaking a complicated idea or problem into simpler parts in an orderly way.
A mind or soul understood as not taking up physical space.

questions_to_think_about: When you learn a skill, do you first learn the facts, or do you also learn where to direct your attention?
Why might touch help someone understand space and objects?
What is the difference between recognizing something familiar and remembering it as past?
Can language help people think, or does it only communicate thoughts they already have?
What problems could arise from claiming that all mental abilities come from sensation?
